case_study_insert.main_stem: Meadowlark Community Care (MCC) is a cooperative in the domiciliary care sector, employing a workforce of 210. Founded in 2004 by Anita Deshmukh, MCC is a member-owned home-care cooperative covering five districts and uses a flat structure with democratic leadership. It plans to invest $640,000 in a new regional care hub in Eastvale and national home-care accreditation, financed by a $400,000 ten-year bank loan and $240,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $765,000 a year, a variable cost of $8.50 a unit and a selling price of $17.00, and currently produces 120,000 units a year. MCC faces carer turnover of 34%, difficult recruitment of qualified carers, complaints about late visits, and a waiting list of new clients.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations and Quality Report — Q3 2025: The five care districts delivered 30,000 home-visit units last quarter; 93.2% of visits arrived within the scheduled 30-minute window, down from 95.1% a quarter earlier. Client complaints fell from 29 to 17 per month. A survey of 700 clients and families found 74% rated carer kindness excellent and 41% would use a dementia-care service line; 58% would pay up to $6 more per visit for weekend cover. Staff turnover is 34%, and 39 of 210 carers have not completed the new medication-awareness training. Off-the-job training at the community college costs $680 per carer.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Meadowlark Community Care for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.5% to 5.5%, the fourth rise this year, increasing borrowing costs for businesses with variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 8.2% from $12.30 to $13.31 per hour from April 2026, the largest rise in a decade, sharply raising care-sector wage bills. (3) Care consumables and travel fuel costs have risen 9.3% year-on-year, care-services inflation is running at 8.6%, and demand for home care grew 5.7% in the same period.

questions.question_text: MCC plans to finance part of its Eastvale care hub with a ten-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for MCC of using retained profit to fund the expansion instead of the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Using retained profit costs MCC nothing in interest or arrangement fees, protecting members' pooled cash flow at a time when the cooperative already carries fixed costs of $765,000 a year and a proposed $400,000 ten-year bank loan commitment. Every dollar not paid as interest can absorb the 9.3% rise in consumables and travel fuel and helps MCC keep home-visit prices accessible to the 58% of families willing to pay up to $6 more for weekend cover, strengthening its case for national accreditation.

Point 2: Retained profit avoids the collateral risk of borrowing against the new $640,000 Eastvale hub, so the $240,000 stays available without risking the hub if member demand disappoints or growth of 5.7% in home-care demand stalls. It also preserves the cooperative's member ownership and democratic control, since no lender can dictate staffing patterns, service standards or the dementia-care service line wanted by 41% of the 700 clients and families surveyed.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Meadowlark Community Care, its Eastvale hub and its accreditation bid.

questions.question_text: MCC is promoting its new Eastvale care hub and accreditation bid. Consider a local newspaper campaign, regional radio sponsorship, or community social media and leafleting. Which should MCC choose to promote the new hub? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Local newspaper campaign: A local newspaper campaign would build credibility with older residents and families in the Eastvale district, many of whom still rely on print for community news, and suits an accredited cooperative with 22 years of local trust since 2004. However, readership is shrinking, and the cost per converted client is hard to track; much of the budget would reach households outside the five districts MCC actually covers, so wastage is significant for a cooperative funding a $640,000 hub partly with a $400,000 bank loan.

Regional radio sponsorship: Regional radio is cheaper than print or national channels and reaches families across the wider area on car journeys, keeping MCC's 30-minute visit promise and accredited status front of mind. However, reach is broad but shallow; radio cannot target the exact households with elderly relatives, and it cannot collect booking enquiries directly, so converting awareness into assessed client intakes would still be slow against complaints about late visits (93.2% on-time, down from 95.1%).

Community social media and leafleting: Targeted social media reaches adult children organising care for parents, while door-drop leaflets reassure non-online families; both evidence MCC's 74% excellent kindness rating and the demand signal from the 41% wanting dementia care. This mix is cheap, trackable through enquiry codes and referral partners such as discharge planners, and directly supports accreditation; it depends, however, on consistent messaging and staff following up enquiries promptly.

Recommendation: MCC should choose community social media and leafleting. It is the cheapest, most measurable option, reaches exactly the local carer-decision segment identified in its research, and reinforces both recruitment and intake for the Eastvale hub. The local newspaper campaign is rejected as untargeted and hard to measure; regional radio is rejected as too broad and too indirect for urgent domiciliary care decisions — both may support awareness, but neither should lead the launch.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of MCC with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of MCC with a well-justified recommendation explaining why the newspaper campaign and radio sponsorship are rejected.

questions.question_text: MCC's carer turnover has reached 34%. Explain two benefits for MCC of using democratic leadership to improve motivation in its home-care teams.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership invites the 210 carers to help shape visit scheduling, travel routing, rota design and the dementia-care service line, rather than simply receiving instructions from the central office. Giving frontline carers a genuine voice raises job satisfaction and meets social and esteem needs, reducing the frustration behind 34% turnover and the pressure on the remaining workforce covering five districts with a growing waiting list of new clients; carers who help design their own rotas are also more likely to cover extra visits at short notice, protecting the 58% weekend-cover demand.

Point 2: Involving carers generates practical ideas from the people who delivered 30,000 home-visit units last quarter and who know why 93.2% of visits arrive on time and why others run late. Suggestion-driven improvements to travel planning, handover notes and medication prompts could cut late visits and complaints (29 to 17 a month), raise retention, lower recruitment costs for hard-to-hire qualified carers and protect the cooperative's plan to grow Eastvale and win national home-care accreditation; continuity of care also reassures families choosing MCC over cheaper alternatives.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to MCC's turnover, visit punctuality, complaints and output.

questions.question_text: MCC must train the 39 carers who have not completed the new medication-awareness training. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the community college. Which should MCC choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Training beside experienced senior carers in real client homes is directly relevant to MCC's exact medication routines, documentation and escalation protocols, costs no fees and keeps the 39 carers visiting clients — vital with a waiting list of new clients and punctuality already slipping to 93.2%. However, it depends on senior-carer availability, can pass on shortcuts in record-keeping, and gives no external certificate that the accreditation auditors and most commissioners expect to see.

Off-the-job training at the community college: College courses at $680 per carer give structured, up-to-date medication-safety skills and formal certificates for all 39 carers at $26,520 in total — modest against a $640,000 hub investment and $765,000 fixed costs. However, staff are absent from visits for days, clients must be reallocated at short notice, content is generic rather than matched to MCC's records system, and travel plus back-fill add strain for a 34%-turnover workforce across five districts.

Decision: MCC should choose off-the-job training at the community college for the 39 carers, supported by brief on-the-job coaching in homes afterwards, keeping momentum on visits while guaranteeing externally audited competence. The accreditation bid and medication-risk profile demand externally verified competence and certificates; on-the-job-only delivery is rejected because inconsistent medication practice would endanger clients, fail the audit and destroy the trust signalled by the 74% excellent kindness rating, while the $26,520 cost is trivial against the hub investment and future contract income — and if budget or scheduling pressure ever forces a choice, the college route still comes first because medication safety is the one area where informal handover cannot be relied on.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to MCC.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of both training methods in the context of MCC.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both training methods in the context of MCC with a well-justified decision tied to client safety, accreditation, cost and waiting lists.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how MCC's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $765,000 ÷ ($17.00 − $8.50) = $765,000 ÷ $8.50 = 90,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 90,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $17.00 − $8.50 = $8.50. Answer: contribution per unit is $8.50.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways MCC's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Compare the 90,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 120,000 units to confirm the cooperative is comfortably profitable with a margin of safety of 30,000 units, informing how the Eastvale hub should staff up in year one.
2. Use contribution per unit of $8.50 to model fee rises or the $6 weekend premium: adding $6 lifts contribution to $14.50, showing how weekend cover wanted by 58% of families could fund extra carers against the 34% turnover.
3. Check that the $400,000 ten-year bank loan is serviceable by verifying the 30,000-unit margin of safety survives the 8.2% minimum wage increase before committing to the $640,000 hub and the accreditation fees.
4. Benchmark unit cost ($765,000 ÷ 120,000 units + $8.50 = $14.875 a unit) across quarters to find districts with cost overruns, challenge travel-fuel inflation of 9.3% and attack the fall in on-time visits from 95.1% to 93.2%.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 90,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $8.50 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety of 30,000 units against 120,000-unit output; weekend-cover and fee modelling against the $765,000 fixed costs; feasibility checking for the $400,000 bank loan funding the Eastvale hub; unit-cost benchmarking at $14.875 to cut fuel inflation and late visits.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate MCC's financial performance by calculating the gross profit margin, the profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has MCC's financial performance improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 35.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 40.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 12.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 15.0%
ROCE 2024 = 14.4%
ROCE 2025 = 17.0%

Detailed workings: 2024 gross profit $630,000 on revenue $1,800,000 (cost of sales $1,170,000); 2025 gross profit $816,000 on revenue $2,040,000 (cost of sales $1,224,000). 2024 operating profit $216,000; 2025 operating profit $306,000. 2024 capital employed $1,500,000; 2025 capital employed $1,800,000. Interest payable rose from $20,000 to $28,000, reflecting the ten-year bank loan for the Eastvale hub.

Evaluation: Underlying performance improved solidly. Gross profit grew from $630,000 to $816,000 (29.5%) as revenue rose $240,000 and cost of sales as a share of revenue fell from 65.0% to 60.0% — helped by complaints falling from 29 to 17 a month and tighter purchasing despite the 9.3% consumables and fuel inflation. Operating profit grew from $216,000 to $306,000 (41.7%), well ahead of revenue growth of 13.3%, so overheads were absorbed efficiently. Capital employed rose $300,000 towards the Eastvale build, yet the return on that capital still strengthened from 14.4% to 17.0%. However, the 8.2% minimum wage rise will bite hard in 2026 for a labour-intensive cooperative, and the 93.2% on-time rate slipping from 95.1% signals operational strain on the districts.

Conclusion: Yes, MCC's financial performance has improved. Revenue, gross profit and operating profit all grew, cost control improved and the return on capital employed climbed from 14.4% to 17.0%. The judgement is not risk-free — wage inflation and visit punctuality need attention — so MCC should finalise the Eastvale hub quickly, push membership and weekend-cover growth, and lock in economies before the April 2026 wage increase.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the gross profit margin, the profit margin and ROCE for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of revenue, cost of sales, interest and capital employed movements and a justified conclusion on whether MCC's financial performance improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for MCC of launching a dementia-care service line at the Eastvale hub.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: A dementia-care service line answers a clear demand — 41% of the 700 clients and families surveyed would use it, and 58% would pay up to $6 more per visit for weekend cover — letting Eastvale differentiate from basic home-help rivals, lift the cooperative's contribution per unit from $8.50 and build a strong case for national home-care accreditation. It also creates a higher-acuity revenue stream to service the $400,000 bank loan while membership grows by 5.7% nationally in home care, and a professionally led dementia pathway strengthens commissioner confidence in awarding Eastvale contracts.

Disadvantage: Dementia care demands specialist training, medication protocols (39 carers have not yet completed medication-awareness training) and tighter supervision, raising variable and training costs beyond the $680 college fee per carer. Missteps carry serious safeguarding risk, could damage the 74% excellent kindness rating, and any audit failure would jeopardise the $640,000 hub investment and the accreditation on which future commissioner contracts depend; MCC would therefore need to phase the rollout behind completed medication training and spot checks.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to MCC's survey data, costs and accreditation bid.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.5%, the 8.2% minimum wage increase and the 9.3% rise in consumables and travel fuel costs will affect MCC. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.5% to 5.5%): On a $400,000 ten-year variable-rate loan, a 1.0 percentage point rise adds about $4,000 a year of extra interest, edging MCC's financing cost above the current $28,000 interest charge. Higher rates also make the remaining funding need for the $640,000 Eastvale hub costlier and could dampen consumer willingness to fund paid weekend cover; the direct cash hit is real but modest for a cooperative part-funded by $240,000 retained profit.

Minimum wage increase (8.2%, to $13.31 per hour): Domiciliary care is labour-intensive; perhaps 120 of MCC's 210 carers cluster near the minimum wage. On a $13.31 hourly base for roughly 2,000 hours a year, the increase is about $2,020 per affected worker, or roughly $242,000 a year across 120 carers — almost matching 2025 operating profit of $306,000 and forcing urgent action on fees, travel routing and productivity, especially with recruitment of qualified carers already difficult and turnover at 34%.

Input cost inflation (9.3% consumables and fuel): Consumables and travel fuel sit inside the $8.50 variable cost per unit; if they account for roughly $2.00 a unit, a 9.3% rise adds about $0.19 per unit. At 120,000 units a year that is about $22,400 of lost contribution annually — manageable through route planning, bulk purchasing and the $6 weekend premium, but another squeeze alongside wage and interest pressure.

Conclusion: The 8.2% minimum wage increase will have the greatest impact. It strikes MCC's dominant cost base — its carers — at roughly $242,000 a year, almost the entire 2025 operating profit, and far exceeding the about $22,400 consumables hit and the roughly $4,000 interest rise. Consumable inflation is the second most serious risk; the interest rise is the smallest, though both still demand tighter wage productivity, fee review and coordinated purchasing to protect the accreditation bid and the Eastvale hub.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to MCC.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on MCC's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of MCC with a well-justified judgement that the minimum wage increase has the greatest impact, and why the consumables rise and the interest rise are smaller.
